Question ten. What is batch normalization, and why does it help? For each mini-batch, it shifts and scales a layer's inputs to mean zero and variance one. This batch has a mean of six point six. After normalizing, zero. Then two learned numbers, gamma and beta, set the scale and the shift the network actually wants. It steadies training, tolerates larger learning rates, and makes the starting weights matter less. At inference it uses running averages instead of the batch. Transformers use layer norm, which normalizes across the features of each example. The last two long ones are about the shape of the network itself.

Question eleven. When do you use a C N N, an R N N, or a transformer? A convolutional neural network slides one small filter across a grid, looking for the same pattern everywhere, so it suits images and audio. A recurrent neural network reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state forward. It fits ordered data, but it's slow, and it forgets over long spans. Gated versions like the L S T M, long short-term memory, forget less. A transformer relates every position to every other at once, in parallel. That handles long-range context, and it's the backbone of modern language models.

Question twelve. What is self-attention? Each token makes a query, a key and a value. Score every query against every key, divide by the square root of their length so the softmax doesn't saturate, and softmax each row into weights. Here are four tokens with random vectors of length four. Every row adds up to one. Each token's output is its row's blend of all four values, and all four rows are computed at once.
